newsitem.title: ICELAND: Volcanic eruption follows Iceland flood.
newsitem.headline: Volcanic eruption follows Iceland flood.

text.p: A volcanic eruption sent clouds of smoke billowing 14,000 (4,300 metres) feet above Iceland on Wednesday, a day after a flood wreaked havoc on an uninhabitated part of the rugged North Atlantic island.

Scientists said it was a followup eruption to a series of sub-glacial volcanic explosions last month that melted water and fed the hidden lake of Grimsvotn. It overflowed on Tuesday to unleash the flood onto a plain of black volcanic sand in southeastern Iceland.
Prime Minister David Oddsson took the floor during a parliamentary debate on the flood to announce the new volcanic explosion.
"We cannot discuss action on the flood damage at the moment because another eruption has started," he said, looking tired.

Both the volcano and the lake are more or less covered by Vatnajokull, Europe's largest glacier. Scientists, their seismographs confused by tremors from the formidable flood, were unsure at first whether the latest outbreak by the volcano was an eruption or just a release of steam.

"This was part of the old eruption," said Ragnar Stefansson, a seismologist of the state meteorological institute. "The build-up of water cooled down the earlier eruption before it was really over. Magma was still unreleased.
"When the water disappeared (in the flood) the pressure was lowered again above this part of the fissure and that was enough to trigger a small explosive eruption," he said.
The outpouring of sub-glacial Lake Grimsvotn sent a torrent of sulphurous black water and ice smashing bridges, flooding parts of Iceland's vital ring road and felling power lines.
The new eruption came as planes and helicopters surveyed the damage done by Tuesday's flood on the coast south of the Vatnajokul glacier.
The flood reached its peak on Tuesday night with water rushing out at 45,000 cubic metres (1.6 million cubic feet) per second, but was reduced to a strong stream on Wednesday afternoon.
Not a trace remained of two bridges, including a 400-metre (1,300 foot) steel and concrete span over the Gigjukvisl river.
The swollen river itself was filled with hundreds of icebergs which were carried several km (miles) downstream by the torrent and helped smash the bridge.
A nearby 900-metre (2,950-foot) bridge over the river Skeidara was partly swept away. Only one of four bridges along the 35-km (22-mile) stretch of the coastal road was undamaged.
Scientists had forecast an outburst from Lake Grimsvotn, but when it finally broke they said the flow of meltwater was faster and much more violent than they expected.

The government had expected the cost to be at least 1.5 billion Icelandic crowns ($23 million) if all bridges were wiped out. But the actual cost to public finances will be limited, as most will be borne by an insurance fund set up by the government after a volcanic eruption in 1973.

Oddsson said the disaster had done great damage to the country's infrastructure because of the importance of the coastal road in freighting fish catches from eastern ports to Reykjavik for export abroad.
"This has put us back 25-30 years to the days when we did not have the bridges and the road," he told reporters.
Companies were considering exporting fish from eastern harbours.
